  • (circumstantial facts) is more reliable for investigation than human statements, as it
  • can be analyzed to establish links between a suspect and a crime, even if indirectly. (2

  • that states that every object, whether natural or man-made, has
  • unique identifying features that cannot be duplicated. This means that
  • no two objects can be exactly the same, even if they appear similar.

  • and consistent operation of laboratories, ensuring the accuracy and
  • reliability of their testing and calibration results. This standard is vital
  • for laboratories as it enhances the credibility of their testing and
  • calibration work, fostering trust among clients and regulatory
  • authorities. Compliance with ISO/IEC 17025 demonstrates a
  • laboratory's commitment to quality, technical proficiency, and
  • scientific rigor.

questions.question: What do you mean by ethics in forensic science?
questions.solution_html:
• Ethics in forensic science is critical to maintaining the integrity of the justice system.
  • Forensic scientists often deal with evidence that can significantly influence legal
  • outcomes, and their responsibilities require strict adherence to ethical principles to
  • ensure fairness, accuracy, and impartiality. 1. Principle of Impartiality, 2. Accuracy and
  • Precision in Analysis, 3. Honesty and Integrity, 4. Confidentiality, 5. Competency and
  • Continuing Education, 6. Avoiding Misleading or Incomplete Testimony, 7. The
  • Principle of Professionalism. (explained)

questions.question: Discuss the Law of Progressive Change. How does this principle relate to evidence collection / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• The Law states that everything undergoes change over time—biological, chemical,
  • and physical. In forensic science, this means evidence deteriorates (blood dries,
  • fingerprints fade, bodies decompose), so timely collection is crucial.It guides
  • investigators to document and preserve evidence before environmental or human
  • factors alter it. (2 marks explanation + 2 marks establishing relation)

questions.question: Discuss the various disciplines within forensic science, such as forensic chemistry, biology, and digital forensics. Explain the methods used in each discipline and provide case studies that demonstrate their application.
questions.solution_html:
• Forensic Chemistry
  • When cases that involve chemicals and chemical reactions are
  • investigated, forensic chemistry is used. It deals with all kinds of
  • adulterations and examines the evidence to make inferences
  • regarding the case. The adulterations that it deals with are food,
  • liquor, petroleum, explosive materials, alcoholic and non-alcoholic
  • beverages, carbonated drinks, packaged juices, and drugs. Apart from
  • these it also examines the adulteration of chemicals and compounds
  • like RDX, PETN, HMX, Nitrogylcerine, Nitrocellulose, Sulphur Oxides,
  • Fuses, Cordite sticks, etc.
  • Forensic Biology
  • Forensic Biology deals with biological evidence-like tissues, blood,
  • muscles, semen, hair, saliva, pollen, urine, etc. It is one of the most
  • important branches of forensics as it deals with living beings.
  • Digital Forensics
  • Digital Forensics involves the recovery, analysis, and investigation of
  • data found in digital devices such as computers, smartphones, and
  • other electronic systems, often for use in criminal investigations.
  • • Recovering deleted files, emails, and chat logs from digital
  • devices.
  • • Analyzing cybercrimes, such as hacking, fraud, or identity theft.
  • • Presenting digital evidence in court to support criminal
  • investigations.

questions.question: Define forensic science and discuss its significance in the criminal justice system. Include examples of how forensic techniques have been applied in high-profile cases to aid investigations. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Definition:
  • Forensic science is the application of scientific principles and laboratory techniques to
  • analyze crime-related evidence for use in courts of law. (2 marks )
  • Significance:
  • Ensures objective and scientific evaluation of evidence.
  • Helps identify victims and suspects.
  • Reconstructs crime scenes and establishes timelines.
  • Enhances reliability of investigations and court judgments. (3 marks)
  • High-profile examples:
  • Nirbhaya Case (2012): DNA profiling and digital evidence identified all accused.
  • Aarushi-Hemraj case: Forensic odontology, blood spatter analysis, and scene
  • reconstruction were crucial. (Detailed explanation 5 marks)

questions.question: Define crime scene and give a detailed note on crime scene management? / [CO3] [1x10 = 10]
questions.solution_html:
• Crime scene:
  • A location where an offense has occurred or where evidence related to the crime is
  • present. (2 marks)
  • Crime Scene Management Steps:
  • Securing the scene: First responders protect life and isolate the area.
  • Documentation: Photography, videography, sketching, and note-taking.
  • Systematic search: Grid/spiral/zone methods to locate evidence.
  • Evidence collection: Proper handling, packaging, labeling, and chain of custody.
  • Preservation: Prevent contamination or loss using PPE and sealed containers.
  • Transport and storage: Evidence sent to laboratory safely.
  • Crime scene reconstruction: Investigators interpret clues to recreate the sequence of
  • events. (6 marks)
  • Importance:
  • Proper management ensures accuracy, prevents tampering, and strengthens the
  • evidentiary value in court. (2 marks)
